title: Dimensional analysis
examples: How do I start checking if an equation is correct?
Can dimensional analysis tell me if an equation is physically possible?
What are the basic dimensions I should remember?

explain.say: Today we will learn about dimensional analysis in physics.
This method uses the fundamental dimensions of physical quantities.
For example, the dimension of speed is length divided by time.
We can use dimensions to check if an equation is dimensionally consistent.
If the dimensions on both sides do not match, the equation is incorrect.

draw.text: Dimensions must match on both sides

faq.q: What are the fundamental dimensions in physics?
faq.a: The fundamental dimensions are usually length, mass, and time. These are the basic measurements we use.

faq.q: How do I check if an equation is dimensionally correct?
faq.a: You must write the dimensions for every term on both sides of the equation. Then you compare them.
asks: Is dimensional analysis for checking equations?
How do I use dimensions to check formulas?

faq.q: Can dimensional analysis find unknown exponents in a formula?
faq.a: Yes, it can help you find the relationship between exponents. However, it cannot determine dimensionless constants.
asks: Can I find the powers using dimensions?
Does it help with constants like pi?

faq.q: What are the dimensions of force?
faq.a: Force is mass times acceleration. So its dimension is mass times length divided by time squared.
asks: What are the dimensions of Newton?

faq.q: Does dimensional analysis work for all physics equations?
faq.a: It works very well for checking consistency. But it cannot check every single aspect of a formula's correctness.
asks: Is it perfect for all physics?
What are the limitations of dimensions?

facts: The dimensions of length are represented by the symbol [L].
The dimensions of time are represented by the symbol [T].
The dimension of velocity is [L] divided by [T].
For an equation to be dimensionally correct, both sides must have the same dimensions.

quiz.why: Work is force times distance. Force has dimensions of mass times length divided by time squared. Multiplying by distance, which is length, gives the correct dimension.

wrong.0: This option incorrectly uses time squared in the denominator.
wrong.1: This option is dimensionally incorrect because it misses the mass unit.
wrong.3: This option forgets the mass component of force.

quiz.say: The dimension of momentum (mass times velocity) is:
quiz.why: Momentum is mass times velocity. The dimension of velocity is length divided by time, so the product gives mass times length divided by time.

wrong.0: This option incorrectly uses length squared.
wrong.1: This option incorrectly omits the mass unit entirely.
wrong.2: This option incorrectly squares the time unit.

quiz.say: If the period (T) of a simple pendulum depends on length (L) and gravity (g), the relationship is T ∝ L^x g^y. What are x and y?
quiz.why: By setting the dimensions of T equal to the dimensions of L and g, we find the exponents that make the equation dimensionally consistent.

wrong.0: This incorrectly suggests the period does not depend on gravity.
wrong.1: This incorrectly suggests the period only depends on gravity and not length.
wrong.3: This assumes a simple linear relationship for both length and gravity.
